lady.  You are not to suppose because she keeps my house for
me, that she hasn’t been very high up the tree—ah, up
at the top of the tree!  Now, if you have got anything to
say that can’t be said before a born lady, this lady will
leave the room.  If what you have got to say  can  be
said before a born lady, this lady will stay where she
is.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's absurd justification for Mrs. Sparsit's presence exposes his snobbery and class anxiety; his language parodies upper-class pretension.
enrichment.best_quote: Now, if you have got anything to say that can't be said before a born lady, this lady will leave the room.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby insists that Mrs. Sparsit is a lady of high birth and will remain unless Stephen has something improper to discuss.

text:
‘Sir, I hope I never had nowt to say, not fitten for a
born lady to year, sin’ I were born mysen’,’
was the reply, accompanied with a slight flush.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's brief, polite demurral; dialogue filler establishing his respect and circumspection.
enrichment.summary: Stephen assures them he has nothing improper to say before a lady.

text:
‘Very well,’ said Mr. Bounderby, pushing away his
plate, and leaning back.  ‘Fire away!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's crude encouragement to speak; minimal content.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby tells Stephen to proceed with his request.

text:
‘I ha’ coom,’ Stephen began, raising his
eyes from the floor, after a moment’s consideration,
‘to ask yo yor advice.  I need ’t
overmuch.  I were married on Eas’r Monday nineteen
year sin, long and dree.  She were a young lass—pretty
enow—wi’ good accounts of herseln.  Well! 
She went bad—soon.  Not along of me.  Gonnows I
were not a unkind husband to her.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's painful disclosure of his wife's alcoholism and degradation establishes the emotional core of his suffering and the reason for his visit; his dialect and restraint make it powerful.
enrichment.best_quote: I were married on Eas'r Monday nineteen year sin, long and dree.
enrichment.summary: Stephen recounts his nineteen-year marriage to a woman who quickly turned to drinking and dissolution, for which he bears no blame.

text:
‘I have heard all this before,’ said Mr.
Bounderby.  ‘She took to drinking, left off working,
sold the furniture, pawned the clothes, and played old
Gooseberry.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's crude interruption; minor dialogue revealing his impatience and prior knowledge.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby interrupts, saying he already knows the details of Stephen's wife's degeneration.

text: ‘I were patient wi’ her.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief affirmation from Stephen; dialogue filler.
enrichment.summary: Stephen affirms that he was patient with his wife.

text:
(‘The more fool you, I think,’ said Mr. Bounderby,
in confidence to his wine-glass.)

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's aside reveals his moral judgment and callousness; satirical moment exposing his character.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby mutters under his breath that Stephen was foolish to be so patient.

text:
‘I were very patient wi’ her.  I tried to
wean her fra ’t ower and ower agen.  I tried this, I
tried that, I tried t’other.  I ha’ gone home,
many’s the time, and found all vanished as I had in the
world, and her without a sense left to bless herseln lying on
bare ground.  I ha’ dun ’t not once, not
twice—twenty time!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Emotionally powerful account of Stephen's sustained suffering, repeated humiliation, and desperate attempts to save his wife; demonstrates his moral character and endurance.
enrichment.best_quote: I were very patient wi' her. I tried to wean her fra 't ower and ower agen. I tried this, I tried that, I tried t'other.
enrichment.summary: Stephen describes his decades of patience, his repeated efforts to help his wife, and the despair of finding everything lost and his wife destroyed by drink.

text:
Every line in his face deepened as he said it, and put in its
affecting evidence of the suffering he had undergone.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrator's direct observation of Stephen's emotional transformation; physical embodiment of suffering makes his pain viscerally real for listeners.
enrichment.summary: Stephen's face shows the deep marks of suffering he has endured.

text:
‘From bad to worse, from worse to worsen.  She left
me.  She disgraced herseln everyways, bitter and bad. 
She coom back, she coom back, she coom back.  What could I
do t’ hinder her?  I ha’ walked the streets
nights long, ere ever I’d go home.  I ha’ gone
t’ th’ brigg, minded to fling myseln ower, and
ha’ no more on’t.  I ha’ bore that much,
that I were owd when I were young.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Escalation of Stephen's suffering narrated in accumulating clauses; includes vivid images of desperation (walking streets, contemplating suicide); poignant expression of endurance despite dehumanization.
enrichment.best_quote: I ha' gone t' th' brigg, minded to fling myseln ower, and ha' no more on't.
enrichment.summary: Stephen describes the worsening degradation of his wife, her repeated abandonments and returns, his desperate all-night walks to avoid home, and his suicidal ideation.

text:
Mrs. Sparsit, easily ambling along with her netting-needles,
raised the Coriolanian eyebrows and shook her head, as much as to
say, ‘The great know trouble as well as the small. 
Please to turn your humble eye in My direction.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Sparsit's response satirizes her pretension and callousness; she equates her marriage troubles (about money) with Stephen's suffering, revealing class-based misunderstanding.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Sparsit responds to Stephen's account by raising her eyebrows and gesturing self-pityingly, implying that the great also know trouble.

text:
‘I ha’ paid her to keep awa’ fra’
me.  These five year I ha’ paid her.  I ha’
gotten decent fewtrils about me agen.  I ha’ lived
hard and sad, but not ashamed and fearfo’ a’ the
minnits o’ my life.  Last night, I went home. 
There she lay upon my har-stone!  There she is!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's revelation that he paid his wife to stay away for five years and that she has returned shows his agency and dignity; the image of her on his hearth is powerfully tragic.
enrichment.best_quote: There she lay upon my har-stone! There she is!
enrichment.summary: Stephen reveals that for five years he paid his wife to stay away, allowing him to regain decency and dignity, but last night she returned and was lying on his hearth.

text:
In the strength of his misfortune, and the energy of his
distress, he fired for the moment like a proud man.  In
another moment, he stood as he had stood all the time—his
usual stoop upon him; his pondering face addressed to Mr.
Bounderby, with a curious expression on it, half shrewd, half
perplexed, as if his mind were set upon unravelling something
very difficult; his hat held tight in his left hand, which rested
on his hip; his right arm, with a rugged propriety and force of
action, very earnestly emphasizing what he said: not least so
when it always paused, a little bent, but not withdrawn, as he
paused.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended and brilliant character portraiture of Stephen's physical and emotional embodiment; the narrator shows his dignity, intelligence, and suffering through meticulous physical detail and emotional depth; a masterpiece of descriptive realism.
enrichment.best_quote: In the strength of his misfortune, and the energy of his distress, he fired for the moment like a proud man.
enrichment.summary: The narrator describes Stephen in vivid physical detail: his momentary flash of proud anger before his characteristic stoop returns, his pondering expression, his careful gestures, all suggesting intelligence wrestling with suffering.

text:
‘I was acquainted with all this, you know,’ said
Mr. Bounderby, ‘except the last clause, long ago. 
It’s a bad job; that’s what it is.  You had
better have been satisfied as you were, and not have got
married.  However, it’s too late to say
that.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's response is dismissive and offers no sympathy; he judges Stephen rather than helps him, establishing his moral bankruptcy.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby says he knew about Stephen's wife's conduct and judges his marriage choice as a mistake, expressing no sympathy or offer of help.

text:
‘Was it an unequal marriage, sir, in point of
years?’ asked Mrs. Sparsit.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Sparsit's question exposes her class bias; she assumes misery must stem from unequal age difference rather than alcoholism or poverty.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Sparsit asks if Stephen's marriage was unequal in point of years, implying that such inequality would explain its misery.

text:
‘You hear what this lady asks.  Was it an unequal
marriage in point of years, this unlucky job of yours?’
said Mr. Bounderby.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby relays Mrs. Sparsit's question; minimal content, transitional dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby repeats Mrs. Sparsit's question about the age difference in Stephen's marriage.

text:
‘Not e’en so.  I were one-and-twenty myseln;
she were twenty nighbut.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's factual reply; minimal narrative content.
enrichment.summary: Stephen answers that both he and his wife were approximately the same age when they married, around twenty-one.

text:
‘Indeed, sir?’ said Mrs. Sparsit to her Chief,
with great placidity.  ‘I inferred, from its being so
miserable a marriage, that it was probably an unequal one in
point of years.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Sparsit's response is absurdly condescending; her expectation that misery requires unequal ages exposes class blindness and inability to understand poverty or labour-class suffering.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Sparsit responds with placidity, saying she inferred the marriage was unequal in years because it was so miserable.

text:
Mr. Bounderby looked very hard at the good lady in a side-long
way that had an odd sheepishness about it.  He fortified
himself with a little more sherry.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's reaction suggests discomfort with Mrs. Sparsit's implication about her own marriage; he drinks more sherry to fortify himself.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby looks at Mrs. Sparsit with an odd, sheepish expression and drinks more sherry.

text:
‘Well?  Why don’t you go on?’ he then
asked, turning rather irritably on Stephen Blackpool.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's impatient prompt; transitional dialogue moving Stephen forward to state his request.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby asks Stephen to continue with his request.

text:
‘I ha’ coom to ask yo, sir, how I am to be ridded
o’ this woman.’  Stephen infused a yet deeper
gravity into the mixed expression of his attentive face. 
Mrs. Sparsit uttered a gentle ejaculation, as having received a
moral shock.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's direct statement of his plea—to be 'ridded of this woman'—is the pivot point of the entire scene; his request for divorce exposes the legal and class inequities that drive the novel's moral argument.
enrichment.best_quote: I ha' coom to ask yo, sir, how I am to be ridded o' this woman.
enrichment.summary: Stephen asks Bounderby how he can be freed from his wife, and Mrs. Sparsit reacts with moral shock.

text:
‘What do you mean?’ said Bounderby, getting up to
lean his back against the chimney-piece.  ‘What are
you talking about?  You took her for better for
worse.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's response cites the marriage vow formulaically; exposes his legalistic thinking and lack of compassion.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby tells Stephen that he took his wife for better or worse and cannot simply discard her.

text:
‘I mun’ be ridden o’ her.  I cannot
bear ’t nommore.  I ha’ lived under ’t so
long, for that I ha’ had’n the pity and comforting
words o’ th’ best lass living or dead.  Haply,
but for her, I should ha’ gone battering mad.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's anguished rebuttal: he reveals that he cannot endure the situation any longer and attributes his psychological survival to the hope of another woman's love; poignant and passionate.
enrichment.best_quote: I mun' be ridden o' her. I cannot bear 't nommore. I ha' lived under 't so long, for that I ha' had'n the pity and comforting words o' th' best lass living or dead.
enrichment.summary: Stephen insists he must be freed from his wife, saying he cannot endure it any longer, and that only the love of another woman has kept him from madness.

text:
‘He wishes to be free, to marry the female of whom he
speaks, I fear, sir,’ observed Mrs. Sparsit in an
undertone, and much dejected by the immorality of the people.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Sparsit's inference makes explicit what Stephen implies; her judgment of the morality exposes class bias and her own moral confusion.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Sparsit infers that Stephen wishes to be free to marry another woman, and expresses moral dismay at such immorality.

text:
‘I do.  The lady says what’s right.  I
do.  I were a coming to ’t.  I ha’ read
i’ th’ papers that great folk (fair faw ’em
a’!  I wishes ’em no hurt!) are not bonded
together for better for worst so fast, but that they can be set
free fro’  their  misfortnet marriages, an’
marry ower agen.  When they dunnot agree, for that their
tempers is ill-sorted, they has rooms o’ one kind an’
another in their houses, above a bit, and they can live
asunders.  We fok ha’ only one room, and we
can’t.  When that won’t do, they ha’ gowd
an’ other cash, an’ they can say “This for
yo’ an’ that for me,” an’ they can go
their separate ways.  We can’t.  Spite o’
all that, they can be set free for smaller wrongs than
mine.  So, I mun be ridden o’ this woman, and I want
t’ know how?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: This is the most devastating critique of marriage law and class inequality in the novel; Stephen's extended argument shows the legal double standard: the wealthy can divorce through expensive legal channels, whilst the poor are trapped eternally.
enrichment.best_quote: When they dunnot agree, for that their tempers is ill-sorted, they has rooms o' one kind an' another in their houses, above a bit, and they can live asunders. We fok ha' only one room, and we can't.
enrichment.summary: Stephen argues that the wealthy can obtain divorces through legal channels unavailable to the poor, and that he therefore deserves the same freedom from an intolerable marriage that the rich enjoy.

text: ‘No how,’ returned Mr. Bounderby.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's blunt refusal is the crisis point; his two-word answer crystalizes the injustice and leads to Stephen's final plea.
enrichment.best_quote: No how.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby gives Stephen a flat refusal: there is no way out.

text:
‘If I do her any hurt, sir, there’s a law to
punish me?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's series of probing questions methodically establishes the legal trap: the law offers only punishments, never solutions; each exchange tightens the vice.
enrichment.best_quote: If I do her any hurt, sir, there's a law to punish me?
enrichment.summary: Stephen asks if there is a law to punish him if he harms his wife.

text: ‘Of course there is.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's confirmation; part of the catechism of legal constraint but minimal new content.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby confirms there is such a law.

text:
‘If I flee from her, there’s a law to punish
me?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's next question; continuation of the legal catechism.
enrichment.summary: Stephen asks if there is a law to punish him if he flees from his wife.

text: ‘Of course there is.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's confirmation; brief element of the pattern.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby confirms there is such a law.

text:
‘If I marry t’oother dear lass, there’s a
law to punish me?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's third question; continuing pattern.
enrichment.summary: Stephen asks if there is a law to punish him if he marries another woman.

text: ‘Of course there is.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's confirmation; continuing the catechism.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby confirms there is such a law.

text:
‘If I was to live wi’ her an’ not marry
her—saying such a thing could be, which it never could or
would, an’ her so good—there’s a law to punish
me, in every innocent child belonging to me?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's most troubling hypothetical: even cohabitation without marriage would be punished; shows his desperation and the totality of the legal trap.
enrichment.best_quote: If I was to live wi' her an' not marry her—saying such a thing could be, which it never could or would, an' her so good—there's a law to punish me, in every innocent child belonging to me?
enrichment.summary: Stephen asks if there is a law to punish him even if he merely lives with another woman without marrying, and if that punishment would extend to their hypothetical children.

text: ‘Of course there is.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's final confirmation in the catechism; brief.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby confirms there is such a law.

text:
‘Now, a’ God’s name,’ said Stephen
Blackpool, ‘show me the law to help me!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's climactic plea is the emotional and philosophical apex of the scene; his invocation of God and demand for justice that protects rather than punishes is the novel's central cry against institutional cruelty.
enrichment.best_quote: Now, a' God's name, show me the law to help me!
enrichment.summary: Stephen, having established that every possible action is illegal, cries out in desperation for a law that would help rather than punish him.

text:
‘Hem!  There’s a sanctity in this relation of
life,’ said Mr. Bounderby, ‘and—and—it
must be kept up.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's non-response appeals to abstract sanctity; exposes his moral bankruptcy and inability to engage with Stephen's real suffering.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby responds that there is sanctity in marriage and it must be kept up, failing to address Stephen's plea.

text:
‘No no, dunnot say that, sir.  ’Tan’t
kep’ up that way.  Not that way.  ’Tis
kep’ down that way.  I’m a weaver, I were in a
fact’ry when a chilt, but I ha’ gotten een to see
wi’ and eern to year wi’.  I read in th’
papers every ’Sizes, every Sessions—and you read
too—I know it!—with dismay—how th’
supposed unpossibility o’ ever getting unchained from one
another, at any price, on any terms, brings blood upon this land,
and brings many common married fok to battle, murder, and sudden
death.  Let us ha’ this, right understood. 
Mine’s a grievous case, an’ I want—if yo will
be so good—t’ know the law that helps me.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's devastating rebuttal directly attacks the hypocrisy of institutional indifference; his passionate argument that the law's enforcement of indissoluble marriage leads to violence and death is the novel's most powerful indictment of institutional cruelty.
enrichment.best_quote: I read in th' papers every 'Sizes, every Sessions—and you read too—I know it!—with dismay—how th' supposed unpossibility o' ever getting unchained from one another, at any price, on any terms, brings blood upon this land, and brings many common married fok to battle, murder, and sudden death.
enrichment.summary: Stephen argues eloquently that the law's refusal to allow divorce drives desperate people to violence, and he appeals to Bounderby to help him find a legal path out of his suffering.

text:
‘Now, I tell you what!’ said Mr. Bounderby,
putting his hands in his pockets.  ‘There  is 
such a law.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby offers hope, then immediately dashes it; the reversal is cruel and structurally mirrors the novel's critique of false promises from authority figures.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby says there is a law that could help Stephen, attracting his attention.

text:
Stephen, subsiding into his quiet manner, and never wandering
in his attention, gave a nod.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's brief, attentive response; minimal content.
enrichment.summary: Stephen subsides into his quiet manner and gives a nod, listening carefully.

text:
‘But it’s not for you at all.  It costs
money.  It costs a mint of money.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: The price is revealed to be prohibitive; Bounderby's revelation that divorce requires vast sums (equivalent to Stephen's lifetime wages) drives home the class injustice at the novel's heart.
enrichment.best_quote: But it's not for you at all. It costs money. It costs a mint of money.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby tells Stephen that the law is available only to the wealthy, as it is prohibitively expensive.

text:
‘How much might that be?’ Stephen calmly
asked.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's calm question; brief dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Stephen calmly asks how much the law would cost.

text:
‘Why, you’d have to go to Doctors’ Commons
with a suit, and you’d have to go to a court of Common Law
with a suit, and you’d have to go to the House of Lords
with a suit, and you’d have to get an Act of Parliament to
enable you to marry again, and it would cost you (if it was a
case of very plain sailing), I suppose from a thousand to fifteen
hundred pound,’ said Mr. Bounderby.  ‘Perhaps
twice the money.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: The staggering cost—£1000-£1500 or more—is rendered concrete; this figure is devastatingly unattainable for a labourer earning perhaps £1/week; Dickens's calculation emphasizes the economic impossibility.
enrichment.best_quote: you'd have to go to Doctors' Commons with a suit, and you'd have to go to a court of Common Law with a suit, and you'd have to go to the House of Lords with a suit, and you'd have to get an Act of Parliament to enable you to marry again, and it would cost you (if it was a case of very plain sailing), I suppose from a thousand to fifteen hundred pound.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby explains the bureaucratic maze required for divorce and names a cost of £1000-£1500, perhaps twice that, which is utterly beyond Stephen's means.

text: ‘There’s no other law?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's final question; his last hope for an alternative path, which will be denied.
enrichment.summary: Stephen asks if there is any other law that might help him.

text: ‘Certainly not.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's final refusal; brief and conclusive.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby says there is no other law.

text:
‘Why then, sir,’ said Stephen, turning white, and
motioning with that right hand of his, as if he gave everything
to the four winds, ‘’ tis  a muddle. 
’Tis just a muddle a’toogether, an’ the sooner
I am dead, the better.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's final pronouncement of 'muddle' is the climactic distillation of the novel's philosophy; his despair and near-suicidal conclusion crystallizes the human cost of institutional indifference and injustice.
enrichment.best_quote: 'tis a muddle. 'Tis just a muddle a'toogether, an' the sooner I am dead, the better.
enrichment.summary: Stephen turns white and declares the entire situation a muddle, saying he would be better off dead than trapped in this impossible legal and social situation.

text:
(Mrs. Sparsit again dejected by the impiety of the
people.)

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Sparsit's brief response; comic contempt for Stephen's despair, revealing her moral blindness.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Sparsit is again dejected by the impiety of the working people.

text:
‘Pooh, pooh!  Don’t you talk nonsense, my
good fellow,’ said Mr. Bounderby, ‘about things you
don’t understand; and don’t you call the Institutions
of your country a muddle, or you’ll get yourself into a
real muddle one of these fine mornings.  The institutions of
your country are not your piece-work, and the only thing you have
got to do, is, to mind your piece-work.  You didn’t
take your wife  p.
59 for fast and for loose; but for better for worse. 
If she has turned out worse—why, all we have got to say is,
she might have turned out better.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's dismissal of Stephen's critique, his defense of institutions, and his demand for deference constitute the novel's central exposure of power's indifference to suffering; his authoritarian assertions ('don't you call the Institutions...a muddle') are repugnant.
enrichment.best_quote: The institutions of your country are not your piece-work, and the only thing you have got to do, is, to mind your piece-work.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby scolds Stephen for questioning the institutions of his country, tells him to focus on his work, and offers platitudes about marriage.

text:
‘’Tis a muddle,’ said Stephen, shaking his
head as he moved to the door.  ‘’Tis a’ a
muddle!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Stephen's reiteration of 'muddle' as he leaves emphasizes his despair and the chapter's central message; his repetition is haunting.
enrichment.best_quote: 'Tis a muddle. 'Tis a' a muddle!
enrichment.summary: Stephen shakes his head and repeats that everything is a muddle as he moves toward the door.

text:
‘Now, I’ll tell you what!’ Mr. Bounderby
resumed, as a valedictory address.  ‘With what I shall
call your unhallowed opinions, you have been quite shocking this
lady: who, as I have already told you, is a born lady, and who,
as I have not already told you, has had her own marriage
misfortunes to the tune of tens of thousands of pounds—tens
of Thousands of Pounds!’ (he repeated it with great
relish).  ‘Now, you have always been a steady Hand
hitherto; but my opinion is, and so I tell you plainly, that you
are turning into the wrong road.  You have been listening to
some mischievous stranger or other—they’re always
about—and the best thing you can do is, to come out of
that.  Now you know;’ here his countenance expressed
marvellous acuteness; ‘I can see as far into a grindstone
as another man; farther than a good many, perhaps, because I had
my nose well kept to it when I was young.  I see traces of
the turtle soup, and venison, and gold spoon in this.  Yes,
I do!’ cried Mr. Bounderby, shaking his head with obstinate
cunning.  ‘By the Lord Harry, I do!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Bounderby's final valedictory is a masterpiece of patronizing hypocrisy; his false profundity ('I can see as far into a grindstone as another man'), his smug reference to his own past suffering, and his baseless suspicions about turtle soup and gold spoons expose his moral blindness and callousness perfectly.
enrichment.best_quote: I can see as far into a grindstone as another man; farther than a good many, perhaps, because I had my nose well kept to it when I was young.
enrichment.summary: Bounderby lectures Stephen about his 'unhallowed opinions,' congratulates himself on his perception, and falsely accuses Stephen of being influenced by agitators and desiring luxury.

text:
With a very different shake of the head and deep sigh, Stephen
said, ‘Thank you, sir, I wish you good day.’  So
he left Mr. Bounderby swelling at his own portrait on the wall,
as if he were going to explode himself into it; and Mrs. Sparsit
still ambling on with her foot in her stirrup, looking quite cast
down by the popular vices.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The final image—Bounderby swelling before his portrait, ready to explode into it, while Mrs. Sparsit sits unmoved—is a brilliant visual and satirical conclusion; Stephen's departure marks the chapter's thematic closure and his own descent into desperation.
enrichment.best_quote: So he left Mr. Bounderby swelling at his own portrait on the wall, as if he were going to explode himself into it; and Mrs. Sparsit still ambling on with her foot in her stirrup, looking quite cast down by the popular vices.
enrichment.summary: Stephen thanks Bounderby formally and leaves, while Bounderby contemplates his own portrait with inflated self-satisfaction and Mrs. Sparsit remains immobilized by disapproval.
